utterances.text: I cannot recollect what I exactly knew about General Mladic at that time but that I knew that he was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The senior on the spot.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The senior -- a very high military officer of the Serb army. That was without a doubt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, since then have you been able to figure out who he is or who he was at the time?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read something about him in the NIOD Report, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And would it be accurate to say that what you said was that he was the highest, not a high ranking but the highest, the top of the top, of all the officers, in other words, he was the top of the military command structure of the VRS? Would that be a fair characterisation?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, from listening to you, based on what you observed, at the scene, on the 12th, it seems to me, correct me if I'm wrong, that we have the highest military officer on the ground acting like a platoon commander, micro-managing and giving orders to anyone and everyone he could get a hold of. Would that be a fair characterisation?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was giving orders when he wanted to, but the process was ongoing and like in every army, when the highest ranking officer comes to the scene and he wants to change anything, he can, because he's the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, when the highest commanding officer of the Dutch army comes to the airport where you're working and he can just give you an order?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he does not like things that are happening, he can give me an order, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But isn't there some sort of a chain of command that he should go to your commanding officer and maybe give him an order to give you the order? Isn't there sort of like a trickle down approach?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he wants to do it in a nice way, he can use the chain of command but he's still a general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now when you say a nice way, are you -- is it nice, polite, being friendly --

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or being correct? What is the correct way?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The correct way is that he is a general and can give orders to anyone he wants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he does not want to go past the chain of command, then he would do it the way you stated and use the chain of command to change things, but when a general comes to Schiphol airport and he doesn't like the way things are happening or maybe some -- even things about discipline, he can give an order. He's still -- he still has a rank of a general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when he gives you that order, he'll take -- you know, you as a hypothetical because I would imagine armies by and large function the same way, they have to, right?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: More or less. They have to have a structure. And when he's giving you that order, I would imagine that you're subordinated to him for that particular task that he's giving you, are you not?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if he tells to you do something and you do it, and let's say, hypothetically speaking, that he asks you to do something that later on proves to be incorrect. I'm not talking about illegal activity but say for instance incorrect, and there is an inquiry, can your superior officer, the one that he bypassed, be responsible for your conduct because you listened to the commander up above?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It more or less depends on what the general gives as an order, but if he gives the order, he is also responsible of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But still the person that gets the order is also responsible for what he's doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Absolutely. But can you, for instance, tell the general, "Why don't you talk to my superior officer? Because I think you need to follow the chain of command here"?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have that option?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, being on the ground, do you think the officers that were with Mladic, based on what you saw the way General Mladic acted and behaved, how often did they did up there and contradict him or tell him to just follow the chain of command, the normal procedure? Did you ever notice that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea how the Serb officers gave orders to each other. I don't know how that happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But you did see Mladic ordering people, including soldiers, what to do?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when he was on the ground, would it be fair to say that he was in charge?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be fair to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nobody else was in charge but him?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was micro-managing, would that be a correct way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of orders he gave out there, and if those were micro-orders or other orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When a general, when the highest general, excuse me, and I'll slow down here for a second, but when the highest general of the army is giving an order to a foot soldier, don't you think that's micro-managing, in your opinion as a military officer being trained in the academy, having all of that experience?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the order he gives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And of course you didn't speak any Serbian, right, so you didn't understand what orders he was giving?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when he wasn't there, there was his second in command, occasionally, sometimes, I believe you referred to him as his -- you thought he might have been his Chief of Staff, gentleman -- Colonel Jankovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. He made an impression on you especially because of his perverse sense of humour always checking up and saying, well, I see that lieutenant, using the Serbian word for it, you're still alive; right?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was sort of an unnerving thing to say at the time and he struck you and he made an impression on you, right?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that when Mladic wasn't there and he was on the ground, that he was in charge?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because at that time I didn't know what role Colonel Jankovic played.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that he was a logistics officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And of course later on, I read in the NIOD Report something about the role and Colonel Jankovic but at that time, I did not know that his role.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. By the way I appreciate the fact that you're distinguishing what you read and what you observed because I think that's what I'm here for. What you observed on the ground there. So when he was on the ground, if I understand you correctly, from what you were able to observe, you could not distinguish whether he was actually in charge or somebody else was in charge or nobody was in charge or everybody was in charge; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that Mane was in charge and Stalin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. We are going to get to them, we are going to get them. But when he was there, your testimony today is the person that you believe that was Mladic's right-hand man, and was right next to Mladic, when Mladic wasn't there you were not sure whether he was in charge?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know at the time that he was his right-hand man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only met him when he was alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But that's what you've indicated that you thought the impression that he gave you that you were able to observe, the dynamics between Mladic and him, as I understand, you got the sense that he was Mladic's right-hand person?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I think I'm going to object to this line of questioning. I don't believe that's precisely what the witness said. He is mischaracterising the evidence and perhaps if the witness can be allowed to explain what he said but that in my respectful submission was a mischaracterisation of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I gave the witness an opportunity, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course the witness has the opportunity to repeat what he said. If there is a mischaracterisation by the Defence counsel, the witness has a right to correct it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I never saw Jankovic and Mladic together. I saw them on separate occasions so when Defence counsel is speaking about Colonel Jankovic and General Mladic together I don't know what he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you say when Mladic came twice -- General Mladic came twice on the 12th, right?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when he came, at least, the first time he had an entourage?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the entourage was basically officers from what you were able to observe?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that there was one officer that looked a little bit like General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. But were there other officers on the ground at the time?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was but I don't remember who they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did any of those officers stay there after Mladic left?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall now, can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You cannot remember. But it's your understanding today, as it was back then, and all the times that you've testified, that this individual named Mane was the person in charge when Mladic wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And might I ask was that an impression that you formed based on your experience and your observations or was that something that was told to you by Mane, in other words Mane said to you, "Lieutenant, I'm in charge"?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now and by that you understood to mean that he was in charge for the situation on the ground at that time?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and also from the things that happened, I told you a story about the guy in the black uniform, I wanted to get away from the Muslim refugees, Mane was the man that could do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Make it happen?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Make it happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when there was a situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, please look at the transcript as well it also applies to the witness. If that sentence is finished with a dot there, you may ask your question, or answer the question. Is that understandable?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: That's too fast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at some point, Mane informed you that his superior was someone by the name of Stalin, he had a nickname or code name Stalin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as I understand it, Stalin showed up at the time, at sometime?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you ever ask Stalin, because as I understand it, you had an interpreter there to assist you, so did you ask Stalin with what unit he was in by any chance?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had a conversation with Stalin, by my recollection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just to be clear, your understanding that Stalin was Mane's superior was from the information that Mane had given you?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, when he -- when Stalin showed up, did Stalin and Mane interact?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I remember. Their interaction was through the radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean they were on the ground and they are talking, they could visibly see each other and they are talking on the radio or this is before Stalin shows up?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before he showed up and Mane knew that Stalin was coming so they had already had contact by the radio before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now when Stalin showed up, if I understand you correctly, Mane didn't go up to Stalin to say, to give him an update and Stalin didn't come up to Mane to get an update? Based on what you were able to observe?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But at some point, you were able to see Stalin speaking with an individual? Someone that you had seen before, someone who was well known, and that individual was Major Nikolic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Because Stalin and Major Nikolic were walking together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I take it that before this day, you had had some dealings with Nikolic or at least you knew who he was by face, that is?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew who he was by face, and that he was responsible for the checkpoint near OP Papa, where all of our convoys, the few convoys we had, passed through, and as I remember, Mane also told me that -- pointed him out, that was Stalin and that was Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have any actual dealings with Major Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know what his actual function was, who he was subordinated to, who he was attached to, who was his commander, what his title was, any of that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was a major, at least that was his rank, and that he was responsible for OP Papa and that was the only thing I knew about Major Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nothing else. So just to make sure that I understand it correctly, you never spoke with Stalin and you never spoke with Nikolic, ever?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you were able to see them on that particular day from afar and you were able to recognise them or it was pointed out to you by Mane that there is Stalin and there is Nikolic, right?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about 25, 50 metres from our location, so it wasn't that far.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 25 to 50 metres?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So that would be about twice the distance from this wall to that wall, is that -- or closer?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how -- what the distance is in this courtroom but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm just asking you to look at it that's why I'm using this as a comparison?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The distance from the courtroom -- the diameter of the courtroom, more or less something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now you never went up to them, close to them?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not closer than that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it you were not able to hear what if anything they were talking about?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, did I not hear that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, would it be fair to say that you could not hear because of the distance? Or were you not just paying attention?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was a combination of the distance, me not talking Serbo-Croatian, and the noise that was on that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. We got all that crowd, right? Now, when you noticed those two individuals, did you lock your sight on to them to kind of figure out what on earth they are doing or you just sort of looked at them and went about the business that you were attending to because after all, you had other things that were more pressing on your mind? Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked at them for a while, because also at that time, Mane was pointing them out to me, so I had a chance to look at them for a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what you were able to see was I guess some hand gestures?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also seeing that Stalin was speaking to Major Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So Stalin was speaking to Nikolic, and as I understand it, maybe I have it wrong, that Nikolic was pointing in some direction or making some hand gestures? Or was he just standing there listening attentively.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were -- they were walking and Major Nikolic was walking in the middle of the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Stalin was walking next to him, and as I remember, Stalin was speaking to Major Nikolic and making some hand gestures, and that gave me the impression that he was explaining something to Major Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We are going to get to that but first, would it be correct to say that Major Nikolic was dressed sort of in a well-pressed uniform, Ray Ban sunglasses, sort of looked very officious, strutting a little bit like a peacock there in the middle of the road? Would that be a correct way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looked like he was inspecting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he also looked officious, did he not?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from the way he carried himself with this sort of aura glowing about himself from what you could see and from what was happening, you discerned that he must be Stalin's superior; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way they two were interacting gave me the impression that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But you could not hear what they were saying and you never talked to them?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I notice that in the military, while you were in the military, you've had the opportunity to visit some countries, including Greece; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are well informed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I'm part Greek, well I am Greek but from America, but when I go to Greece I see people talking with their hands, you know. Could you tell me, when you were in Greece, were you able from 50 yards away to discern what the individuals, what people were talking about when they are their gesticulating, waving their hands, acting about?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm objecting to that, it's totally irrelevant. It's totally irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, drop this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me walk you through some of your statements on this issue because I think this is fairly critical on what has been marked as Defence Exhibit number 7 for identification, that's the one that -- the redacted or the summary from the Royal Netherlands Army, the debriefing, on page number 2, and I believe it says -- it's the third paragraph, it starts with July 12th and it states that you saw Major Nikolic here. At the very last part, the last sentence, within this paragraph, you say, "But Nikolic was Stalin's superior." Now, it doesn't say that you thought it was his superior, that you got that impression but that he was. Do you recall whether that was the statement that you gave or was that the way it was just merely summarised?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a summary, and it also is a translation, and as I try to recall, I think I told that I had the impression that Nikolic was Stalin's superior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could go to Defence Exhibit number 8 for identification purposes, this is the questionnaire that you filled out. I believe you indicated that it was -- when you got to Zagreb, perhaps that early. So shortly after the events. If we flip to page 2, and you can see that there is a list of questions, and I want to take you to the third question from the bottom. And it states, the question is describe anyone who appeared to be in command of them. You're referring to all sorts of people. Including the commanders' name and rank, if you're aware of it. And you say, platoon commander Mane, and this company, company commander, nickname Stalin, of the military police, who arranged the deportation, okay? Now, right after that, there is another question, and this is identify and/or name any other captors, if you can? And you say, "Major Nikolic who was also frequently present." Over here, you do not have him above in the previous question stating that your impression was that Nikolic was the commander of Stalin who was the commander of Mane; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to Defence Exhibit number 9 for identification purposes, over here I've looked for that to see where you state anything about Mane, and Nikolic, and if we flip to page 8, you talk about Stalin at one point being there where he held the formation I guess at the end of the day, I believe that you saw him making roll call or -- but I don't see anything in this statement -- maybe I'm wrong but I don't see anything where you referred to Stalin as Nikolic's subordinate?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you explain to me what exhibit number 9 is?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this was the statement that you provided on October 25th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if page 7 and 8 is where you talk about Mane and at the last paragraph at page 7, and then page 8 you talk -- you do indicate that Stalin came at one point and had an U formation, the men stood and he took roll call, and I believe that -- this is the -- in this particular statement you have the dates wrong. I think you're a day off.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The roll call was on the evening of the 12th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Right. Because then you go on the next day, Thursday the 14th but the next day was actually Wednesday, the 13th?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right but here you don't say anything about -- about Stalin being under Nikolic or that being your impression.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This interview was in a fashion of question-answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that I did not mention it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you did -- when you did testify at the Krstic case, and you have the transcript there available, I'll direct you to page 1746, it was Thursday, 30 March, 2000, and around page -- around line 7, you're asked, or line 6 you're asked -- line 7, now, are you aware -- were you aware at the time who Stalin was subordinated to, who was the commanding officer of Stalin was at the time? And the answer is: "I recall that I'd seen the soldier with the code name Stalin before, together with Major Nikolic. It looked to me that Major Nikolic was the commander of the guy named Stalin because Major Nikolic was in the middle of the road, Stalin was next to him more or less explaining, I couldn't understand what they were talking about because they were talking Serbo-Croat but it really looked to me like Major Nikolic was more or less inspecting what was going on there and Stalin was telling him about everything that happened." So from that, I understand that you -- that was your testimony then and I take it that is your testimony here today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But from reading this, it seems to -- you say that you couldn't understand Serbo-Croatian, that doesn't say that they were so far you couldn't even hear what they were talking about, does it?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it was a combination of the distance and the language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the noise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's the impression that you have?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whether it's actual fact or not, that's the impression that you have but you don't know for certain to this day whether Stalin was under Major Nikolic, do you?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never looked it up in the NIOD Report. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And I believe you also asked later on in the testimony about it and you indicated the same, that basically that was an impression that you had made -- you had formed and that was the end of that; is that correct? Basically, I mean, there is nothing more we can talk about that issue other than it's just an impression that you made and it could be true and it could be false? The impression, that is.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the idea that I got from the things that I had seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we talked a little bit about General Mladic and so as you indicated, he was the highest ranks officer or the highest ranking officer on the scene at the time, right? And -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the times he was present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the times that he was present, okay. And you also indicated yesterday that at one point he made a rather racist comment. Do you recall that, with respect to the Dutch and the multi-ethnicity and the one soldier who happened to be black? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, to be honest with you I was thinking about that last night and I'm wondering whether the reason that it was posed, the question was posed to you was whether -- was because you wanted to give the impression that somehow all the soldiers that were there shared the same sentiments, the same racist sentiments that General Mladic had indicated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's totally inappropriate, it's irrelevant and speculative. I just don't see where all this is going. I think Mr. Karnavas's cross-examination is getting a little repetitive, quite frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I have the same impression, Mr. Karnavas, would you please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well but for the record, Your Honour, this was raised by the Prosecutor in order to inject the issue of racism into the Court so I'm just merely wanting to get the witness to clear up the issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, getting back to the report, the time that you were questioned before the parliamentary committee, there was one particular issue that you were questioned somewhat about and that was an omission on your part earlier to state that you had seen passports that were being discarded, that you had testified today that you collected. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recall that. It was no omission on my part because I mentioned it in my debriefing report in Assen. It was an omission to take that from my debriefing report into the big report, the summary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I stand corrected on that but as I understand from reading the material and even during the hearing, you were questioned whether on the scene you had brought that to your superior's attention, your commander's attention?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether I have -- that was a question, if I had radioed in and told the story about the passports by radio. That was the question of the inquiry committee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And my understanding was that you had failed to provide that information at the time, on the scene.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not give the information by radio because I thought that was not necessary to give that by radio. I just wanted to stress that we should accompany the buses from the -- and that was my goal and it was not necessary to elaborate on that and tell them about passports or any other things I had seen. That's why I made a choice not to tell the passports because as I stated at the committee, if you talk to each other by radio, you try to keep the message that you are sending as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But did you tell that to Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans sometime thereafter when you next saw him or was this something that you brought to the attention when you gave your statement at the Assen committee?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was -- I'm sure I mentioned it at the committee in Assen and I don't know if I have mentioned it earlier to other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans get into trouble at all as a result of not having that information passed on to him by you at the time? That's just a question. It's not a trick question.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, you don't know. Is that something that he should have known, given that he was there on the scene? I mean here was vital information that you had and him being the commander, isn't that something that he should have known?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that the question of finding passports changed anything about the men being separated from the women and being --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm going to interrupt you here. You're not answering the question. The question was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, we actually haven't heard the rest of the answer, Your Honour, so we don't really know if the witness is answering the question. I think he should be given the opportunity to finish his answer before being interrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course, witness you may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As an officer I'm trained to think about what a commanding officer should know, what is relevant information for him, and at that time, I did not think that the information about the passports had anything -- any more information in it than the pure fact of the men being separated from the women and the men being transported separately from the women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, you made a judgement call at that point in time given your training that this was not relevant information?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Relevant information --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or necessary information.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was relevant to know that the buses should be accompanied and to stress that we would do everything we had to try and accompany the buses and to say anything about passports would not make the accompanying of the buses more or less needful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But work with me here for a second. I'm not judging whether what you did was correct or incorrect. I'm merely stating what I seem to understand coming from you. That information wasn't passed on as a result of you thinking given the situation on the ground wasn't that pertinent at that particular moment. You made a judgement call based on your training and based on what was happening, right?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made the judgement call to stress that we should accompany the buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you also made the judgement call not to inform Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans, right, that it wasn't necessary at that particular time?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have a direct line with him, with Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was he at the time?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was at the UN headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At our headquarters at the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was the UN compound?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So he wasn't there in -- he was only a few kilometres away, right?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And reachable by radio, right?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not direct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not direct but you could reach him. Now, hypothetically speaking, okay, this is a hypothetical, what if - and I'm not suggesting that it is - but what if that information was critical and I'm not suggesting for one moment that it is, that it was, but what if that information was critical? Given his location, and given where you were, is that something that Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans would have known since he was the commander on the scene at the ground at that time?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what you mean about what he would have known. Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, as a commander he's supposed to know everything that's happening, you know, at least that's what some would have us believe, that as the highest commanding officer on the ground he should know what all of his troops are doing at any given time, what information they may be possessing. Given that situation, as it was happening and the judgement call that you had to make and everything else, do you think it would have been possible for Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans to have known that somehow you had that -- you were in possession of that information?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans exactly was at the time that I found the passports so you should ask him that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you. Is that something that he should have known given where he was located and given the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the information he needed to give orders to the rest of the troops that we still had, then the information of me stressing that we should accompany the buses was enough for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And the information regarding the passports you decided he didn't need, at least, at this particular moment?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that moment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any cross-examination, Ms. Sinatra?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour I do have cross-examination that should take maybe 30 minutes but I would like to ask the understanding of the Trial Chamber just for a second. I just got passed a message from Mr. Stojanovic with some questions on it that I haven't had time to understand or ask. May we take a ten minute break while I prepare just for one more second? Just to clarify what this is. If it's too difficult, Your Honour, I will try to punt but I really can't decipher what this message is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any way, we will have our break in about 20 minutes so why don't you go on with the questions you have prepared and then during the break, you could consult with your colleague.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: That's perfect, thank you, Your Honour. I'm sorry, how does this work because I need something that will catch the papers? I'm sorry, this is arranged incorrectly. Thank you very much. Cross-examined by Ms. Sinatra:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Lieutenant Van Duijn, is that how you pronounce your name?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Van Duijn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Van Duijn, okay. Thank you very much. I would just like to follow up with a few questions. When you said you were stationed with Charlie company in Srebrenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Charlie company was stationed at the compound in Potocari and for the last period, I was stationed -- I was under the command of Captain Groen from Bravo company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bravo company was at OP...?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Srebrenica compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Srebrenica. So if you said you had to establish these blocking positions on the road from the Swedish housing project to Srebrenica, and these blocking positions included cooperation and close air support from UNPROFOR? Wasn't that the original decision?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were UNPROFOR, of course, and we had to take up blocking positions so that we would with our APCs and our own weapons, the .50 calibre machine gun on the APC, and the rest of our weapons, small calibre and anti-tank rockets, together with air support, try and stop the Serb advancement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just to make this clear, D7, which is the parliamentary committee report from November 11, 2002, that has been marked as D7-1, I will be referring to this repeatedly so if you would like to take it out in front of you it may assist in my questions. But you talk about the green versus the blue order. In fact, in your parliamentary questioning, you did state that you were totally undermanned and it was not realistic to have a green order at that time, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is that in the report?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's on page 5 of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra, are you sure it's D7?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the stenographic report. I believe it's D7-1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No it's D10.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: D10, I'm really sorry. D10-1. Thank you for correcting me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you show me what page or paragraph that was?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, well, let's go to page 6 and the question from Mr. Bakker was, "You therefore took up these blocking positions, did you think this was realistic at the time?" And you said, "We -- a green order with the material we had was actually not realistic." That's what you said in the questioning?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But -- and you didn't have any orders from any superiors at that point and you gave the order to your gunners to open fire when you saw the Serbs at that time, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was an of course a constant flow of orders and information that was given from me to Captain Groen and the other way around of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your purpose of opening fire at that time even though you were undermanned and this was not realistic was so that you could get the air strike cover, right?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was to -- that was to make a statement that -- to the Serbs that they would notice that we were there, and that we were not going away and firing for them to stop their advancement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's your statement today that you did not use this opportunity as a vehicle to get the air cover that you were -- had been requesting?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not my use of my vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that was your understanding when you went out there for the blockades, wasn't it, blocking positions?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My order was to take up a position and to stop the Serb advancement and together with air support, make a stand and stop that advancement, and it was not my intention to draw fire with my APC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if Pieter Boering has stated that that was one of the purposes of the blockades, of the blocking positions, he would be incorrect; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were more vehicles in the blocking position and later on, I heard that our battalion had the intention of using our vehicles to draw, more or less, draw fire, but that was not my understanding of my order that I got at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't have good communications with your superiors at that point; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had communications by radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they didn't tell you the true motive of this operation?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have that order, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that your anti-tank weapons were useless at that point. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were -- it was more or less a danger to the soldier that would shoot or use the anti-tank weapon because they were indicators on it for humidity and they had passed the accepted level. So it was more or less a danger to fire the anti-tank weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they would have been exploding in your hands, then? Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a possibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on page 11 of your statement -- not your statement but this parliamentary inquiry, last paragraph, you stated that you took over the command from the lieutenant who was sitting on the verge, and I also took over the walkie-talkie that was on the battalion's radio network and I immediately came under the battalion's command. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What part of the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last paragraph on page 11. Actually the last two sentences.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the verge, did you mean that he was on the verge of a breakdown?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say that you took over the walkie-talkies and joined the battalion's radio network, you had a system in place at your battalion command centre that kept you in contact with one another, intercepted radio communications from the BH Army and from the VRS army, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The network we used was the units was divided in units so the Bravo company could talk to each other by radio without Charlie company hearing, and from Charlie company of course the same, and so there was also network that was used only by the battalion headquarters and that's what I meant with the network that was used by the battalion headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the battalion headquarters they had telephone operators and equipment for receiving and intercepting other radio communications, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you came under the command of the battalion's radio network, can you tell me who was in charge of that network? Did you speak to one particular person at that time?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were changing operators and at some point I had contact with Major Franken but I didn't have contact with one particular operator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't remember a name that was part of that radio network?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Franken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Franken, okay?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you were aware that on the 13th or the 12th, a huge Bosnian column formed, right? Of Bosnian men, soldiers, women, that were going to leave the Srebrenica area and flee toward Tuzla? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the night of the 11th, when we were with APCs near point 02 waiting for Sergeant Mulder to come from OP Mike to the compound in Potocari we saw a column of soldiers leaving from point 02 towards Susnjari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the 28th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which unit that was. It was a combined column of men, I even recognised a little boy from 12 or 13 years old that lived, used to live near OP Quebec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many soldiers did you see armed?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that must have been about 30 soldiers that were armed and the rest, like the little boy, were not armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But from your radio communications, did you have the information that this column was heavily armed in its trip to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're aware of the agreement that Colonel Karremans entered into with General Mladic that the VRS would provide buses and trucks if the DutchBat commander would provide fuel for the transportation of the refugees? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the only convoy of refugees that was escorted totally out of the area, was that the one that was escorted by Pieter Boering?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if that was the only one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had no knowledge of how many other escorts were given to the refugee convoys?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to go to the 13th. You took the morning of the 13th; is that correct, early in the morning, you took it upon your own initiative to go ahead and load the refugees and get things going that morning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were no VRS soldiers around, right?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, that night before they told you they were going to go celebrate in Bratunac, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they told me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did it ever cross your mind instead of loading the refugees on to the buses, to let them escape?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no place to escape to, and refugees did not make any effort to walk away. If they wanted to walk away, there was -- there was opportunity for that but they stayed where they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying they were like a herd of docile cattle?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that. No, they were scared and they were panicked and they were in need of water and food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given the descriptions of incidents that you had heard from Lieutenant Koster, would it have been wise to have tried to get them taken away yourselves on the buses the night before, before the VRS returned?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: With buses? What do you mean with the buses in the evening? We did not have control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Over the buses?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over the buses, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. On page 20 of this statement that you have, the interview, isn't it true that Lieutenant Koster didn't want you to facilitate the loading of the buses?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also read in the NIOD Report when it came out so not that long ago, that he was -- he did not want the transport to start. What I remember from our discussion we had, that he asked me, well, do you think it's wise to start? And in my recollection, we left it at that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't that an indication that he was questioning your judgement at the time?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was questioning my judgement, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, just one second. Give the court reporter a tiny break.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't personally see any murders or beatings or mistreatment in the Potocari area, did you?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depends on what you understand on the mistreatment. Like the incident I told you about the boy being practically strangled, you can differ about that of course but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to refer you to your statement of October, 1995, which is D7-1. On -- I believe on the last page, page 4, it says that you did not see any men being ill-treated. I believe in your statement before that you said that the only death that you saw on page 3 was a woman who died during child birth in the factory?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the statement of October?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's this one. It's the summary of your statement to Major Gert [phoen], I think was his name. And on page 3 you said that -- page 3, at the bottom, the witness knows a woman who died during child birth but he does not know of any other Muslims who died in the area, and I believe that another one of your statements in your interview says that the only bodies you ever saw were along the road from the blocking area to Potocari and those were casualties of battle. Isn't that what you stated before?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is that --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just going to say it's a little confusing. I'm just wondering if perhaps counsel can point specifically to the areas where she is referring to and then ask the question as opposed to asking the two questions in the manner that she just did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's the correct procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can go back to your statement to Major Gert that you have in front of you, on page 3, didn't you state that "He does not know if any other Muslims died in the place that you didn't see any other deaths at that time"? And this was debriefing shortly after July 20th, when you left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: This is the fifth line from the bottom. On page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then on page 4, if you go halfway up the page in the text, it says, "He did not see any men being ill-treated here." Is that what you stated shortly after you left Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I stated, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then I'd like to go to your statement, back to the statement with the parliamentary committee, on page 21, when asked by Mrs. Huizinga-Heringa, "Did you also see such things yourself?" Your answer: "No, I didn't see any massacres or liquidations myself." Question: "Or bodies?" Answer: "I did see bodies lying on the ground but they had nothing to do with these matters. I saw these bodies on the side of the road as a result of the hostilities on returning from the blocking position. In that sense, this had nothing to do with the transportation of refugees." Isn't that what you stated to the committee?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll resume at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We were just talking about the bodies along the road from the Swedish housing project to Srebrenica or Potocari. You didn't make any report about that, did you?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was from the location from the blocking position back to Potocari, and I don't know if I made report earlier than the debriefing in Assen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to go back to Mr. Karnavas had many questions concerning Mladic, Stalin, Nikolic and Mane. I just want to know if you're clear on the fact that Mladic and Nikolic were part of the military structure of VRS? Were you clear on that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was clear on that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know the difference between the military structure and the military police, which is the ministry of the interior?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: By now I've read a few things about it, in the NIOD Report, but at that time, I all -- I took them all for Serb soldiers, so being part of one big Serb army, more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But now you know that Stalin and Mane were part of the military police, right?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me by then they were military police, but like in the Netherlands, military police is also a part of the Defence force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you know now that that's not true in Republika Srpska, right?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read a few things about that but I don't know what -- what is the exact -- what was the exact location of the officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you also if you've ever heard of this term, Main Staff, in the VRS military structure?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard of the term General Staff from the VRS. Main Staff I've never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Staff was that part of Mladic's domain?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, the staff from General Mladic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That would be out of Pale?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to clarify something else. MUP, which I described just then, military -- the ministry of the interior, they are special police, they are not military police, so I made a mistake. I was just informed about that. Do you know the difference? Have you heard the difference between special police and military police? So you may have been correct in your interpretation of that.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read a few things about it in the NIOD Report but the only thing I know was that Mane stated to me that they were military police and not what sort of branch or something else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, when you were working with Mane, and I assume that you all had a fairly close working relationship during the last few days of the 8th, 9th, 10th, 11th, 12th and 13th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only on the 12th and the 13th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were working closely with him on those days, right?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me if they were uniformed personnel that were working under Mane?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't recognise any insignias on their shoulders or anything?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I remember, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you have been referring to Stalin as a major. Were you familiar with their markings? You've been calling him captain, I think. Were you familiar with the markings on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what rank Stalin was. Mane said he was a captain. But I don't know what rank Stalin wore and I did not see it from his uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he may have had no markings on his uniform whatsoever, right?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated in your earlier testimony that Stalin and Mane communicated by radio communications, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's true that Nikolic had a radio communications device also, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember if he wore it or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or a telephone or a radio that he was using?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go to the point where all the other refugees were gone but there were, as I think you testified to, 20 or 30 men left at the white house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember was that the white house was packed and don't know what my other estimations were about the number of men, but when I think about it now, think back, there must have been two, maybe -- somewhere between 200 and 300 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the white house?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the white house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men did you see sitting in the front of the white house?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: With their backs against the front of the white house, there must have been around five or ten and the rest were sitting inside the white house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they were taken away that evening of the 13th, I suppose, in the truck, that truck was a civilian vehicle that had delivered bread earlier, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No that was on the 12th, and the men from the white house, the white house was only used on the 13th, and the men from the white house were transported with buses and the men from the front lawn of the two houses adjacent, the zinc factory, they were transported with a lorry, a small truck, that I'd recognise from bringing bread earlier that day but that was on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was a civilian truck that took them on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a civilian truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to go back to your report to the parliamentary committee and if you would look at page 21, please? I believe you stated in the third paragraph up, where it has your name, that the Serbian units were known for their phone tapping techniques. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was what we got in the training prior to our deployment in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so if Pieter Boering had said that they didn't have any communications and he didn't know anything about Serbian capabilities, he wouldn't be telling the truth, would he?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he was there during the training when we had that part of the training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You stated in your testimony today, going back to Mane, that Mane was baffled that you were loading the buses, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, Mane, Lieutenant Koster and Lieutenant Rutten were all baffled that you were loading the buses, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if Lieutenant Koster was baffled but Lieutenant Rutten was and I don't know if Lieutenant Rutten knew about the precious one and a half hour in the morning of the second day, the transport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's go to Lieutenant Rutten on page 36, please, of your parliamentary report. Not to 36, I'm sorry. I think that it is -- I'm really sorry, I'm jumping way ahead of myself so if you'll -- I want to go to page 26 of your report while we are there. On page 26, you talk about the operation of separating the men from the women, as something that you would do and that is commonly done in military situations such as this. Didn't you say on page 26 halfway up, that if you think about it, this is exactly what we do? If you want to collect information, you have to separate certain groups of prisoners of war and therefore keep the men apart to find out what information they can provide. So separating the men was not such a strange thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm going to object to that. I think that's taken out of context. Perhaps Ms. Sinatra could start reading the question before the remaining answer so we could be put into context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, maybe you could read this paragraph. This answer again to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness can verify this one way or the other, and I intend to ask to have this introduced into evidence so the Trial Chamber will be able to see everything in its complete context but if you'd like for me to read the question, I will be happy to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The moment which you started to fear the worst for the fate of the Muslim men was when you found the pile of identity cards. Before that you tried to go with them and escort the buses. Did you believe the statements made by the Serbs?" And your answer: "At the time, I believed the statements made by the Serbs --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: "-- that they were removing the men to find out whether they were war criminals. If you think about it, this is exactly what we do. If you want to collect information, you have to separate certain groups of prisoners of war and you therefore keep the men apart to find out what information they can provide. So separating the men was not such a strange thing to do." Is that what you testified to?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said and you have to see that in the context of when you have prisoners of war, then you put them into groups, you put soldiers together with other soldiers, you put officers together with others officers to find information within that group. So you make groups of the big group of prisoners of war so that was more or less like the instructions we have and we do when you have prisoners of war and treat them according to the convention of Geneva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it gave you the presumption that this -- or the appearance that this was a legitimate military operation, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the idea I got, but you must not forget that we were no longer in control so the only option I had was to find out what they were going to do and if they had done it in a military operation, it would not be very strange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't that what you said in your statement, right?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to go back to this page 26. You testified earlier about the location and your finding the passports and personal belongings of the men in the white house after the transport had already been completed, right?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The rest of your testimony about this, to complete the story, is that you actually went and picked up all these passports and stuffed your trousers full with them, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then after that, you went to speak to Mane, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then after you spoke to Mane, you left those passports at the house, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I did that before I spoke to Mane or after that, but like I stated to the parliamentary inquiry committee, I had no explanation for leaving the passports at the site. I don't remember why I did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to go back to the part where it's consistent all the way through this document that you found those passports, you had custody of those passports, you spoke to the Serbian commander but you didn't come away with the passports, did you?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not take the passports with me, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that you stated today in your testimony that you did not think that it was relevant information for Colonel Karremans to have at that moment, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The story about the passports, you meant?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. That was your prior testimony today.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you didn't report the story about picking up the passports and having them all in your control when you were debriefed in Zagreb, did you?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a military debrief and I don't know if I mentioned it there but I assume that was not the case because the debrief was not about the stories around the events but more about the military operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, in your debriefing in Assen, you didn't exactly tell the whole story about the passport incident, did you?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know I told it there, the whole story, I don't know how complete it was getting into the debrief report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if it was left out of General Van der Windt's report then it was a tactical strategy, strategic decision on the part of your commanders, wasn't it?
